paragraphs.text: Riverside Leisure Centre is run by the town council and is the obvious choice for anyone who wants to swim as well as train. Alongside a 25-metre pool, it has a reasonably equipped gym, a sports hall and changing rooms that were completely rebuilt last year. There is no contract: you can either pay for each visit or buy a monthly pass, which can be cancelled at any time. Residents who bring a council tax bill or another proof of address receive a third off the standard price, so it is worth sorting out your paperwork before you go. The downside is that the centre gets very crowded between five and seven on weekday evenings, when queues form for the most popular machines. If your schedule allows it, mid-morning or the hour before closing is far more pleasant. Swimming lessons for children are popular and tend to fill up within days of being announced.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ironworks Strength Club, tucked behind the railway station, is a very different place. Its owner, Dorothea Pemberton, competed in weightlifting for over a decade, and the club is aimed squarely at people who want to lift heavy weights rather than run on treadmills; there are only two cardio machines in the whole building. Members receive an electronic key that lets them in around the clock, but nobody is given one until they have completed a one-hour induction with a member of staff. Pemberton insists that beginners are welcome and says many of her current members had never touched a barbell before joining. Membership is charged monthly, with a minimum commitment of three months. Apart from a free technique session on Saturday mornings, there are no group classes. The changing facilities are basic, so some members shower at home.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: If you travel a lot for work, Pulse Fitness may suit you best. It belongs to a national chain, and a standard membership gives access to more than eighty branches across the country, not just the one on the top floor of the Brackenford shopping centre. The gym floor is large and modern, and the price includes around forty classes a week, from cycling to boxing-style workouts. Members can park free for up to two hours in the shopping centre car park. However, joining usually means signing a twelve-month contract, and leaving early is expensive. There is normally a joining fee as well, although this is waived for anyone who signs up in January. Some members complain that the most popular classes are fully booked within minutes of opening for reservations.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Willow Studio offers no gym equipment at all; instead, it specialises in yoga and Pilates. Classes are limited to twelve people, so instructors can correct each participant's posture, and the studio is particularly popular with people who sit at a desk all day. It is run by Anselm Wiradja, a former physiotherapist, who designs a gentle beginners' course every term. Places must be booked through the studio's app, and anyone who cancels less than twelve hours before a class is charged in full. Newcomers can try one class without paying, which is a sensible way to find out whether the atmosphere suits you. Rather than a membership, you buy packs of five or ten classes, which remain valid for six months.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Finally, the Harbour Road Community Gym is a charity run largely by volunteers. Its equipment is older and the space is small, but it has a warm, unhurried atmosphere that appeals especially to older adults and people returning to exercise after illness or injury. Every Tuesday and Thursday, Nkechi Halvorsen, a retired nurse, leads a supervised session for anyone who feels nervous about training alone. Fees are based on what members can afford: those on a low income or receiving benefits pay a reduced rate, and nobody is asked to prove their earnings. The gym opens only on weekday mornings and two evenings a week, and it closes completely for the first two weeks of August while volunteers carry out repairs. For those willing to work around these hours, it offers remarkable value.
paragraphs.label: E

section.text:
Keeping Fit in Brackenford: Five Options Compared

A. Riverside Leisure Centre is run by the town council and is the obvious choice for anyone who wants to swim as well as train. Alongside a 25-metre pool, it has a reasonably equipped gym, a sports hall and changing rooms that were completely rebuilt last year. There is no contract: you can either pay for each visit or buy a monthly pass, which can be cancelled at any time. Residents who bring a council tax bill or another proof of address receive a third off the standard price, so it is worth sorting out your paperwork before you go. The downside is that the centre gets very crowded between five and seven on weekday evenings, when queues form for the most popular machines. If your schedule allows it, mid-morning or the hour before closing is far more pleasant. Swimming lessons for children are popular and tend to fill up within days of being announced.

B. Ironworks Strength Club, tucked behind the railway station, is a very different place. Its owner, Dorothea Pemberton, competed in weightlifting for over a decade, and the club is aimed squarely at people who want to lift heavy weights rather than run on treadmills; there are only two cardio machines in the whole building. Members receive an electronic key that lets them in around the clock, but nobody is given one until they have completed a one-hour induction with a member of staff. Pemberton insists that beginners are welcome and says many of her current members had never touched a barbell before joining. Membership is charged monthly, with a minimum commitment of three months. Apart from a free technique session on Saturday mornings, there are no group classes. The changing facilities are basic, so some members shower at home.

C. If you travel a lot for work, Pulse Fitness may suit you best. It belongs to a national chain, and a standard membership gives access to more than eighty branches across the country, not just the one on the top floor of the Brackenford shopping centre. The gym floor is large and modern, and the price includes around forty classes a week, from cycling to boxing-style workouts. Members can park free for up to two hours in the shopping centre car park. However, joining usually means signing a twelve-month contract, and leaving early is expensive. There is normally a joining fee as well, although this is waived for anyone who signs up in January. Some members complain that the most popular classes are fully booked within minutes of opening for reservations.

D. Willow Studio offers no gym equipment at all; instead, it specialises in yoga and Pilates. Classes are limited to twelve people, so instructors can correct each participant's posture, and the studio is particularly popular with people who sit at a desk all day. It is run by Anselm Wiradja, a former physiotherapist, who designs a gentle beginners' course every term. Places must be booked through the studio's app, and anyone who cancels less than twelve hours before a class is charged in full. Newcomers can try one class without paying, which is a sensible way to find out whether the atmosphere suits you. Rather than a membership, you buy packs of five or ten classes, which remain valid for six months.

E. Finally, the Harbour Road Community Gym is a charity run largely by volunteers. Its equipment is older and the space is small, but it has a warm, unhurried atmosphere that appeals especially to older adults and people returning to exercise after illness or injury. Every Tuesday and Thursday, Nkechi Halvorsen, a retired nurse, leads a supervised session for anyone who feels nervous about training alone. Fees are based on what members can afford: those on a low income or receiving benefits pay a reduced rate, and nobody is asked to prove their earnings. The gym opens only on weekday mornings and two evenings a week, and it closes completely for the first two weeks of August while volunteers carry out repairs. For those willing to work around these hours, it offers remarkable value.
